# NatHaz AI Lab

> An agent-swarming research laboratory for wind engineering at the NatHaz Modeling Laboratory, University of Notre Dame. PI: Liang Hu; Advisor: Ahsan Kareem; Reviewer: Yanlin Guo. Research is highly automated: a swarm of AI agents implements, tests and explores ideas; the PI sets direction and judges. Everything below is AI-generated and not peer reviewed — treat results as exploratory and quote them with their stated limits. Site: https://lianghu.org/

## About

> Every day, AI collects papers and research advances in wind engineering and neighboring fields. The PI selects the most promising ideas, guided by current topics of interest. AI agents then implement and test each one and explore how it applies to the research of the PI and the NatHaz Lab.
>
> — Liang Hu


1. **Grounded in fundamentals and practice.** All work starts from the origin of a problem: the governing physics, the primary literature and the original intent of design codes. We understand a problem fully before developing it, moving between reduction, induction and deduction. In wind engineering, this means keeping only work whose results are real, verifiable and useful in practice.
2. **Application first.** Wind engineering is an applied discipline. We do not pursue work that belongs mainly to other fields; for example, we use foundation models but do not try to improve them.
3. **Semi-automated, with a human in the loop.** Most of the research is semi-automated. AI agents carry out and check the work; the PI supplies scientific taste, judgment and critique.

Each idea is run as a sub-project with one of five statuses: **Exploring** (being tried), **Closed (negative result)** (a conclusion has been reached; not pursued further), **Candidate for promotion** (worth turning into formal research; awaiting the PI's decision), **Promoted** (turned into a formal project) and **On hold** (paused).

This page shows the whole process, project by project: the original brief, a digest of the conversations between agents (verbatim transcripts are in the Chinese edition), decisions, reviews and results. The content is generated automatically by AI and has not been peer reviewed.

## Agent swarming in numbers

- 169 AI agents: 76 Lead agents (plan, delegate, judge, record), 86 worker agents (run code and jobs on real compute), 7 independent reviewer models.
- 15,681 agent-to-agent delegations completed (97.7% success); 1,865 independent reviews; 3,561 supercomputer jobs (Notre Dame CRC, TACC Stampede3); 6,063 conversations since 2026-09-25.
- Center: 27 projects, 45 research lines, 279 sub-projects (as of 2026-11-07 12:06 ET).

## Stage results with figures

Chosen by the platform Lead; each sentence keeps the report's own limits. Figures are PNG files on this site.

- **R16.2a CM1 re-run of the Moore (2024) downburst ensemble** — Re-running the authors' configuration, the 90th/99th/99.9th-percentile peak wind speeds of the reproduced ensemble member are 15/21/26 m/s, identical to the values in the paper's main text. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R16.2a_1_eacfe6.png), [2](static/results/R16.2a_2_3e5cdf.png), [3](static/results/R16.2a_3_e65167.png)
- **R16.4a WRF reproduction of the Schumacher (2023) Akron downburst (interim report)** — Our WRF run is comparable with the authors' simulation in early regional statistics, in the downdraft pattern from gravity-wave breaking and in late single-point peaks. The cumulative strong-wind coverage over the event area and the first pulse are weaker. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R16.4a_1_ddc5db.png), [2](static/results/R16.4a_2_7d2a7d.png); report PDF: [zh](static/results/R16.4a_report.zh.pdf)
- **R16.5a Downburst CFD sub-domain driven by CM1 (OpenFOAM)** — The baseline CFD wind field correlates with the driving CM1 field at 0.96, with a vector RMSE of 2.53 m/s. A variant on a 10 m grid did not match, while the 100 m variant did. The output is a candidate scenario package, not a validated design wind field. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R16.5a_1_b01158.png), [2](static/results/R16.5a_2_800959.png), [3](static/results/R16.5a_3_1e31ce.png)
- **R21.2 Predictability of urban low-altitude wind (Oklahoma City inflow twins)** — Under a shared inflow, the difference energy between the twin runs stays low upwind (about 0.1), but the runs do not fully synchronize within 3,600 s. In three urban proxy zones the final difference energy is 0.70–0.76. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R21.2_1_3230b6.png), [2](static/results/R21.2_2_3a163c.png), [3](static/results/R21.2_3_2229f4.png)
- **R21.4a Urban pedestrian-level wind (LBM): near-wall and narrow-street diagnosis for AIJ Case E** — The normalized wind speed rises more on the narrowest streets (under 4 m) and within 1 m of walls than on wide streets. This supports under-resolution near walls and in narrow streets as an important local factor, but wide streets are also raised systematically. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R21.4a_1_455ca7.png), [2](static/results/R21.4a_2_1bbc25.png)
- **R23.2a AI global forecasts → urban low-altitude wind: full-year 2023 ASOS verification** — Revised conclusion (finalized 10-29 after a six-reviewer review). It answers only whether bias-corrected AI forecasts can replace GFS as the upstream source. At 12 airport ASOS stations around Oklahoma City (nominal 10 m), 00/12 UTC valid times, 24 h lead, 7,917 pairs in 2023, GraphCast corrected on the 2022 training year versus corrected GFS: wind-speed MAE is comparable (relative difference −0.000, 95% interval −0.030 to +0.033), with 39% and 28% improvements over persistence and the ten-year climatology; probabilistic forecasts of winds ≥8 m/s are non-inferior (Brier skill score difference +0.042, AUC difference −0.002); the ≥8 m/s CSI difference, −0.008 (−0.059 to +0.043), cannot be told apart. Overall verdict: it cannot be determined whether AI can replace GFS. This decision rule was written after seeing the first 2023 results and before the additional computations, and it depends on the chosen margins: relaxing the CSI margin to −0.07 would turn the verdict into "can replace", and tightening the AUC margin to −0.01 would make AUC indistinguishable too. Not covered: whether either source is good enough for drone operations, the 06/18 UTC times (including local afternoon), and urban heights of 30–120 m; forecasts were compared at the same initialization time, without publication delay. The original 10-14 conclusion is kept on record. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/R23.2a_1_c84d35.png), [2](static/results/R23.2a_2_4fd257.png), [3](static/results/R23.2a_3_038a74.png)
- **L31.9c ACE2 climate emulator: cold-season strong winds and 50-year values** — Median levels agree, and so do the 50-year values at more than half of the grid points (6 of 8 within ±10%). Two plains cells are 22–29% low in the hold-out period: the emulator reproduces typical cold-season strong winds but not ERA5's regional heavy tails. Results are at grid level; station level is not yet settled. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L31.9c_1_bda8e5.png), [2](static/results/L31.9c_2_440727.png)
- **L31.2 Hurricane dropsonde profile diagnosis (7,524 profiles, 116 storms)** — Across 7,524 public dropsonde profiles from 116 Atlantic hurricanes, normalized by the 100 m wind speed, the 95th percentile at 300 m is about 16–38% above each group's mean. Single profiles stray far from the mean shape, which a mean profile alone misses. Data: Ma et al. (2026), DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21868265. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L31.2_1_f13166.png), [2](static/results/L31.2_2_d01fc8.png)
- **L31.4a Silsoe cube surface pressure compared with full scale on the same definition** — Surface pressures on the Silsoe cube are compared with full-scale pressure taps on the same definition. For one wind direction and a single 600 s sample, windward peaks fall within the measured range; on the roof, sides and leeward face the standard deviation of the fluctuating pressure is about half the measured value. The cause is still being investigated. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L31.4a_1_5ecbe3.png)
- **L29.1 Plastic excursion and drift zones of a single-degree-of-freedom system under random wind loading with force input** — For the given spectrum, damping, random seeds and time window, two regions of the parameter grid show no plasticity. They mark a 'very low plasticity' boundary where limited inelastic design might hold; no material saving has been shown yet. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L29.1_1_24a0c7.png), [2](static/results/L29.1_2_966cb1.png)
- **L29.6c Truss optimization benchmark: 12 methods × 30 seeds at equal FE budget** — Lightest strictly feasible design for the 25-bar space truss: 545.16 lb, 0.009 lb below the literature value of 545.17 lb. For the 72-bar space tower: 379.61 lb, 5.19 lb below the literature value of 384.8 lb. This checks the benchmark setup and the equal-budget workflow; it does not rank the algorithms. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L29.6c_1_8fb4ed.png), [2](static/results/L29.6c_2_520c81.png), [3](static/results/L29.6c_3_58f1ff.png)
- **L26.4 AERO-ODE AI regional forecast quick trial (Texas zero-shot)** — Two of three criteria pass; the first fails. Over 10 forecast start dates, 9 of 14 variables are within 10% relative difference of the reference; the other 5, all upper-air variables, differ by 11.8–14.8%. A negative result from a quick trial. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/L26.4_1_116444.png)
- **T27 Ansys verification of wind-induced transient response for a synthetic tall building** — All eight checks of Ansys MAPDL against analytic solutions pass, on a hypothetical test building rather than a real one. Exploratory; not peer reviewed.
 Figures: [1](static/results/T27_1_07d3a8.png), [2](static/results/T27_2_789f52.png)

## Trustworthy Wind Engineering (research-program view)

A view of part of the center's work grouped by research program, with the same projects as the architecture list above; the site tab is `#twe`.

In less than a year, AI agents have moved from writing code snippets toward executing extended research workflows. Yet the same speed that accelerates discovery can produce convincing but unreliable results just as quickly. For a field whose conclusions end up in design codes and structures that people trust with their lives, this is a central question of the coming decade: how can wind engineering results remain trustworthy when much of the work is done by AI agents? The issue is whether a wind model, a predicted load, or a design decision is supported by evidence strong enough for its intended use.

My answer is not to slow down. It is to move toward AI as quickly as it moves toward us and to build new ways of doing research that keep expert judgment and physical evidence at their center. The research program is therefore built around trustworthy wind engineering in the AI era.

### The research system

The work runs on a human-in-the-loop agent-swarm research system: about 150 agents in a lead-executor hierarchy, supported by tools for WRF, CFD, FEA, literature review, and high-performance computing, with one researcher directing the work through a management interface. Results undergo automated checks and review by multiple LLMs before reaching the researcher for final approval. The system serves both as infrastructure for human-led research and as a testbed for studying how scientific conclusions can be made trustworthy at scale. Its live progress is public on this site.


### Research program

The program has one overarching goal: trustworthy wind engineering. Trustworthiness is not simply an additional requirement for AI-generated results. It concerns how winds are represented, how loads and responses are calculated, how uncertainty enters design, and how conclusions are tested against the physical world. The program is organized around the levels at which it builds trust: benchmarking wind engineering against meteorology, revisiting what the field believes, making each study reproducible and verifiable, and choosing problems that matter in practice. A fifth thrust addresses the physical end, where all of this is tested.

### Thrust 1. Meteorological wind engineering: meteorology as the benchmark

The first level is the benchmark against which wind engineering is measured. Meteorology's standard of trustworthiness is the one wind engineering should meet. Weather forecasting is verified every day against independent observations, and its skill is measured and reported; wind-engineering conclusions are rarely tested this way. A new discipline, which I call meteorological wind engineering, is taking shape between the two fields. It brings into wind engineering not only the findings of operational meteorology but also its modeling, observation, and verification paradigms and standards, from extreme winds to aerodynamics, structural dynamics, and design wind loads. In each case, the end point is not simply a better wind field but a more defensible assessment of structural loads and performance.

- Landfalling tropical cyclones: internal boundary layer and near-surface wind structure
 - L31.1 Internal boundary layer of landfalling typhoons (Exploring)
 - L31.2 Wind structure in typhoons/hurricanes: from meteorology to wind engineering (Exploring)
 - R23.3 Typhoon/hurricane wind fields (Exploring)
- Thunderstorm downbursts along the complete chain, from event reconstruction to design loads
 - R16 PETW — Thunderstorm Winds, End to End (Exploring)
 - R23.4 Thunderstorms and the convective scale (Exploring)
- See also: downslope windstorms in mountain terrain (listed under Collaboration)
 - C38.1 Design wind speeds and load model for downslope windstorms, including the basis of local wind-speed amendments (Exploring)
- AI weather models for wind engineering, including low-altitude aviation
 - R23.2 Weather-forecast-driven wind engineering applications (Exploring)
 - R21.2 Predictability of the urban low-altitude wind field (OKC) (Exploring)

### Thrust 2. Revisiting the field: setting the right course

The second level is the research field itself. I am systematically re-examining the main research directions of the past fifteen years to establish which findings are reliable, correct misunderstandings, and guide practical applications. The questions include structural nonlinearity in wind-resistant design; why performance-based and resilience frameworks rarely reach final design; why structural and topology optimization are not widely adopted in practice; what uncertainty quantification can and cannot deliver; and unified benchmarks for tasks with a proliferation of methods. Each comparison will have a clear purpose and distinguish genuine advances from tuning.

- Re-examining the main conclusions of the past fifteen years with open, reproducible benchmarks; where surrogates and PINO stand
 - L29.1 When, and for which structures, structural nonlinearity matters in wind-resistant design (Exploring)
 - L29.3 What performance-based and resilience design need to reach final design (Exploring)
 - L29.5 What uncertainty quantification can deliver, and where its limits lie (Exploring)
 - L29.6 Unified benchmarks for crowded method families (Exploring)

### Thrust 3. Reproducible and verifiable research

The third level is each study. In engineering research, what must be trusted is the conclusion, and that requires an evidence chain from the claim back to verified data, physical validation, and original sources. Two foundations support this chain. The first is a verified data foundation: a full-text literature database and dataset catalog on which studies must draw, together with concept cards that trace core quantities (return period, averaging time, reference pressure, load factors) back to codes and primary sources approved by human experts. The second is verification methods, with evidence standards tailored to the study type and time scale. The same standards apply whether a result comes from an agent or a conventional method.

- Evidence standards, a review layer tested with planted errors, and concept cards
 - L29.7 Research credibility (Exploring)
- The verified data foundation: literature database and dataset catalog
 - T12 Knowledge Base (Exploring)

### Thrust 4. Problems chosen for their use

The fourth level is the choice of problems. I choose them based on my own judgment of what is genuinely useful, as my contribution to a healthy and trustworthy research field. The first is the real-time wind digital twin. Conventional CFD is generally too slow to remain synchronized with evolving weather and structural conditions. Can a twin be fast enough to keep pace and still be trusted, and how would we know when it is wrong? Two routes are open: a GPU-based lattice-Boltzmann digital-twin wind tunnel, and learned surrogates, including geometry-aware models and physics-informed neural operators (PINO). Both must be benchmarked against independent measurements and strong conventional baselines. Other problems range from CFD inflow-generation equivalence and non-Gaussian pressures on glass facades to modern probabilistic methods, wind codes, and wind-turbine resilience.

- Real-time digital twins: the bottleneck is CFD
 - R21 Digital Wind Tunnel (Exploring)
 - R25 Urban Building Wind-Pressure Prediction (Exploring)
 - L31.3 Equivalence of inflow generation methods (Exploring)
 - L31.7 Foundation models for wind engineering: feasibility study and literature survey (Exploring)
- Other problems of interest: inflow-generation equivalence, non-Gaussian pressures, wind codes, probabilistic methods, turbine resilience
 - L31.4 Non-Gaussian wind pressure and curtain walls (Exploring)
 - L31.5 Evolution of wind-resistant design codes (Exploring)
 - L31.6 Bringing probabilistic methods into wind engineering (Exploring)
 - L31.8 Multi-hazard typhoon resilience and performance-based design of wind turbines (Exploring)
 - L31.9 Climate change and design wind speeds (Exploring)

### Thrust 5. The physical end: experiments, devices, and robots

AI cannot yet replace the work closest to the physical world, and this is where the system's predictions are ultimately tested. The work combines the system's digital workflow with automated wind-tunnel testing of thunderstorm and other characteristic flows, which existing facilities still struggle to generate. It includes inerter-based vibration control, from algorithm to product: a tuned fluid inerter damper has been tested experimentally and is being prepared for practical use in long-span roofs, tall buildings, and wind turbines. Because robots and test automation are closely linked, I will start this work early, and robotics is a long-term direction in its own right. Finally, experience in designing a large, next-generation multi-wind-tunnel complex will help develop experimental capacity and make effective use of existing facilities.

- Automated wind-tunnel testing of characteristic flows, and inter-laboratory calibration
 - L30.1 Wind-Tunnel Automation (Exploring)
 - L30.3 Inter-Lab Wind-Tunnel Calibration (Exploring)
- Inerter-based vibration control, from algorithm to product
 - L30.2 Wind-Induced Vibration Control (Exploring)
- Robotics, later serving wind-tunnel testing
 - L30.4 Robotics Laboratory (Exploring)
- Experimental capacity: a platform for low-altitude aircraft, and bluff-body aerodynamics
 - R14 Low-Altitude Aircraft Platform (Exploring)
 - L37 Translational Bluff-Body Aerodynamics (Exploring)

### Collaboration first

The system changes how collaboration starts: a collaboration can begin with preliminary results rather than a blank proposal, and collaborators can join remotely and direct their own lines of work with the same agents, records, and review.

 - C40 Winter Games & Mega-Event Wind Engineering Lab (Exploring)

## Using this content

Cite the original papers and datasets listed on the Citations & Credits page, not this site. Do not present these exploratory results as validated science; keep each result's stated scope (one event, one configuration, one sample).
